body:
What is digital evidence?

Digital evidence is information in electronic or digital form that may help establish facts relevant to an incident, complaint or legal proceeding.

Digital evidence may show that a communication occurred, a transaction was made, an account was accessed or a file was altered. However, evidence must be interpreted in context. Its existence does not automatically establish that an offence occurred or prove who committed it.

Digital records may be stored on phones, computers, servers, communication platforms or systems maintained by service providers. Some information is visible to an ordinary user, while other records may be available only to authorised organisations or investigating authorities.

Common examples of digital evidence

  • Messages and emails: Communications that may show what was requested, claimed or threatened.
  • Transaction records: Bank statements, payment confirmations, transaction reference numbers and the recorded date and time of payment.
  • Screenshots: Images of messages, account notifications or other relevant information displayed on a device.
  • Account and access records: Available login notifications or records that may indicate unusual account activity.
  • Website or profile details: A suspicious website address, account identifier or other information associated with a suspected incident.

Different records answer different questions. A payment receipt may establish that a transaction occurred, but it may not establish whether the account holder was deceived. A message may show an impersonation attempt, but further investigation may be needed to identify its sender.

Why preservation matters

Digital information can be deleted, changed or become unavailable. Preserving the original information, where possible, helps investigators examine its source and context.

A citizen should retain relevant communications and transaction details, avoid altering screenshots or documents, and provide accurate information about when and how the records were obtained. If a device may contain important evidence, the person should seek guidance from the appropriate authority before erasing, formatting or unnecessarily changing it.

Protective action and preservation can proceed together. For example, a person may need to secure a compromised account promptly while retaining available notifications and related records. Evidence should be supplied only through appropriate and verified reporting channels, particularly when it contains personal or financial information.

Authenticity and reliability

A digital record must be assessed for authenticity, meaning whether it is genuinely what it is claimed to be. Investigators may also examine its completeness, accuracy and relationship to other records.

A screenshot can be useful, but it may omit the surrounding conversation or other necessary context. A displayed name may be an impersonated identity. A recorded time may require confirmation against other records. These possibilities explain why investigators evaluate evidence rather than treating every digital image as unquestionable proof.

Digital evidence is not automatically conclusive evidence. Its relevance, authenticity and admissibility must be considered under the applicable law.

Chain of custody as a basic concept

Chain of custody refers to the documented history of how evidence was collected, held, transferred and handled. Its purpose is to help establish that the evidence presented can be connected reliably to the original material.

For an ordinary complainant, the practical lesson is simple: preserve the original records where possible, avoid unnecessary alteration and accurately identify the source of material supplied to the police. Detailed forensic examination is the responsibility of authorised specialists and investigating authorities.

Electronic evidence under Indian law

The Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023, which came into force on 1 July 2024, governs matters of evidence in Indian legal proceedings, subject to its application and transitional provisions.

Section 61 provides that an electronic or digital record is not to be denied admissibility merely because it is electronic or digital. Section 63 sets out conditions governing the admissibility of specified electronic-record outputs, including the relevant certificate requirements where applicable. For evidence tendered under section 63, the certificate in the Act's Schedule must accompany each submission for admission and be signed by the person in charge of the device or relevant activities and an expert.

The distinction is important. The law recognises electronic records as possible evidence, but this does not mean that every file or screenshot is automatically proved to be genuine or that every type of electronic record is subject to an identical method of proof.

Evidence and police investigation

When a suspected cybercrime is reported, the police may examine communications, financial records and other relevant material according to law. Investigators seek to establish whether an offence occurred, what conduct was involved and who may be responsible.

A complaint is an allegation that requires appropriate examination. An investigation gathers and assesses evidence. A court determines the legal consequences through the judicial process. These are separate stages, and an accusation does not itself establish guilt.

Fair criminal procedure is particularly important when digital material is involved because records may contain incomplete information or be attributed to the wrong person. The constitutional requirement of fair procedure remains relevant to cybercrime investigations and trials.

Prelims focus

  • Digital evidence may include messages, transaction records, screenshots and electronic account records.
  • Authenticity concerns whether a record is genuinely what it claims to be.
  • Chain of custody concerns the documented handling of evidence.
  • The Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 came into force on 1 July 2024.
  • Section 61 concerns recognition of electronic or digital records; section 63 concerns specified conditions for admissibility.
  • Trap: Electronic form does not make evidence inadmissible, but it also does not automatically prove the truth of its contents.

[Sources: Government of India, Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023, India Code edition as on 6 October 2025, sections 61-63 and commencement provisions; Ministry of Home Affairs, National Cyber Crime Reporting Portal, Frequently Asked Questions and Citizen Manual for Reporting Other Cyber Crime, guidance on supporting material; NCERT, Social and Political Life – III, Class 8, chapter 6, Understanding Our Criminal Justice System, 2018-19 printing, printed pp. 72-75, on investigation, evidence and fair trial; NCERT, Indian Constitution at Work, Class 11, chapter 2, Rights in the Indian Constitution, printed pp. 26-30, on constitutional protection of rights. Official online sources consulted 16 November 2026.]

pictures.alt: A digital record retains its source, time, original information and context through preservation, receipt, investigation and court assessment, with handling documented.
pictures.caption: The usefulness of digital evidence depends on its source, preservation, context and lawful examination.

title: Digital Evidence: Preservation, Investigation and Legal Significance

body:
Why some information systems require special protection

Not every computer system has the same importance to society. A temporary failure of an ordinary website may inconvenience its users. The failure of a system supporting an essential public function may have much wider consequences.

Electricity networks, healthcare services, financial systems, transport facilities and government service-delivery platforms depend on information and communication technology. Serious disruption to certain systems may affect public safety, economic activity or national security.

This is the reason for the concept of critical information infrastructure.

Meaning under the Information Technology Act

Under the Information Technology Act, 2000, critical information infrastructure (CII) refers to a computer resource whose incapacitation or destruction would have a debilitating impact on national security, the economy, public health or safety.

The definition concentrates on the consequences of losing the computer resource. It is not based simply on whether a computer is expensive, whether its owner is a government department or whether many people use a website.

The listed consequences are alternatives. A debilitating impact on public health or safety may be sufficient to bring a computer resource within the definition; every listed type of harm need not occur together.

Understanding the consequences through examples

Electricity services

Digital systems may support the monitoring and administration of electricity services. A serious disruption to an important system could interfere with essential operations and affect households, hospitals or other public services. This creates a connection between information-system security and physical public welfare.

Healthcare services

Hospitals may rely on digital records and communications to deliver care. Loss of access to essential information or systems can interfere with treatment and coordination, with possible consequences for patient safety.

Ports and transport

Large transport facilities may depend on digital communications and information systems. Disruption may affect movement of goods, economic activity and the functioning of connected services. This is particularly relevant when considering Gujarat's ports and industrial activity.

Government digital services

A state data centre may host applications used for public administration and citizen services. A major disruption could prevent many users and offices from accessing necessary information or completing public-service transactions.

These are illustrations of why such systems may be important. They do not establish that every computer, website or application in the electricity, healthcare, transport or government sector has automatically been designated as protected critical information infrastructure.

How digital disruption can affect daily life

A cyber incident may begin as a problem in an information system but have consequences beyond computers. If a shared digital service becomes unavailable, multiple government offices may be unable to use it. Citizens may then face delays in obtaining certificates, submitting applications or accessing other benefits.

The relationship between a digital system and the services depending on it is therefore an important factor in assessing the seriousness of a cyber incident.

Legal protection and responsible institutions

Section 70 of the Information Technology Act, 2000 concerns protected systems and contains the statutory concept of critical information infrastructure. The appropriate Government may, by notification in the Official Gazette, declare a computer resource that directly or indirectly affects the facility of CII to be a protected system; importance alone does not establish formal notification.

Section 70A enables the Central Government to designate a national nodal agency for critical information infrastructure protection. The Government designated NCIIPC for this purpose through a notification dated 16 January 2014.

Section 70B separately concerns CERT-In and its national cyber incident-response functions.

Critical infrastructure protection: NCIIPC, section 70A.
National cyber incident response: CERT-In, section 70B.

Gujarat's critical government information systems

Gujarat's Gujarat State Data Center (GSDC) is located in Gandhinagar and supports the hosting of state government applications and information services.

The Gujarat Security Operations Center (GSOC), established in May 2022, monitors and helps protect important state government information infrastructure deployed at GSDC. The Gujarat Department of Science and Technology identifies cooperation with agencies such as CERT-In and NCIIPC as part of its security arrangements.

Gujarat's electricity services, ports, industries and government information systems provide useful examples of why cybersecurity and essential-service protection are connected. Whether a particular resource is formally covered by a specific legal designation must still be established from the relevant notification or official classification.

Security involves prevention and continuity

Protection of important systems requires attention to both preventing harmful incidents and reducing their consequences. Institutions must be able to recognise problems, communicate with responsible authorities and maintain or restore lawful services safely.

For citizens, the central lesson is that an incident affecting an essential service should be reported through the appropriate channels rather than treated merely as a personal inconvenience. For departments, the lesson is that technical security supports public welfare and continuity of administration.

Prelims focus

  • CII is defined by the potentially debilitating impact of incapacitation or destruction on national security, the economy, public health or safety.
  • Section 70 of the IT Act concerns protected systems and the statutory concept of CII.
  • Section 70A concerns the national nodal agency for CII protection.
  • NCIIPC was designated by notification on 16 January 2014.
  • Section 70B concerns CERT-In and cyber incident response.
  • Trap: An important sector's every computer is not automatically a formally protected system.

[Sources: Information Technology Act, 2000, sections 70, 70A and 70B, Government of India and India Code; Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology, Gazette of India notification S.O. 18(E), 16 January 2014, designation of NCIIPC under section 70A; Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology, National Cyber Security Policy, 2013, Preamble, paragraphs 3-6; Government of Gujarat, Department of Science and Technology, Projects and Initiatives, Gujarat State Data Centre and Gujarat Security Operations Center sections, website updated 27 October 2026. Official online sources consulted 16 November 2026.]

pictures.alt: A shared service outage blocks offices and may delay citizen services; seriousness depends on importance and impact, while an outage alone does not prove cybercrime.
pictures.caption: A serious disruption to a shared digital service can produce wider consequences for public administration and citizens.

title: Critical Information Infrastructure and the Security of Essential Services
